newsitem.title: USA: Freeh says has mulled quitting as FBI chief.
newsitem.headline: Freeh says has mulled quitting as FBI chief.

text.p: Louis Freeh said on Sunday that he had thought about quitting as director of the troubled Federal Bureau of Investigation and that the FBI's general counsel also may leave.
"I've certainly thought about that, but my work in the FBI has been very satisfying," he said in a wide-ranging interview on the NBC television program "Meet the Press."

Freeh, who has served 3-1/2 years of a statutory 10-year term as FBI chief, said he disagreed with an in-house investigation that cleared General Counsel Howard Shapiro of wrongdoing for giving the White House a pre-publication copy of a former FBI agent's scathing book about the Clinton White House.
"Now, my own view of it is that it was not a prudent thing to do, given the perception that has evolved in those very sensitive interactions," Freeh said.

The FBI's Office of Professional Responsibility, which investigated Shapiro's handover of ex-agent Gary Aldrich's book, found that the general counsel had no political motivation for doing so and was guilty of no misconduct.
But Freeh said the FBI, which is probing possible crimes involving President Clinton's Democratic Party fund-raising practices, must be "very, very sensitive to White House contacts."

Asked whether Shapiro was "here to stay" as general counsel, Freeh said: "I don't know. That's up to Mr Shapiro, and he certainly is free to leave the FBI when he determines that that's appropriate. But that's a decision that he's in the process of making."
Freeh also made the following points:
-- That mechanical failure now appears more likely to have caused the mid-air explosion last July of TWA Flight 800, not sabotage.

-- That the FBI still had not been allowed to interview suspects held by Saudi Arabia in the June 25, 1996, truck bombing of a U.S. military housing complex in Dhahran. Freeh said the Saudi approach was typical of many U.S. allies in criminal cases.
-- that U.S. law-enforcement authorities were still awaiting requested permission from Canadian courts to interview a Saudi suspect held in Canada for his alleged role in the Dharhan bombing.
-- that 38 or so FBI agents, backed up two dozen support staff, are involved in a "major investigative effort" into China's alleged effort to illegally buy influence with U.S. officeholders.
-- that at least 23 foreign countries, including some U.S. allies, are actively involved in economic espionage against the United States.
-- that the FBI appears unlikely to be able to identify the person who disclosed the name of Richard Jewell, the one-time suspect in the Atlanta Olympic bombing.
Freeh, a father of five, joked he might not be able to finish out his term if he had more babies.
"Five kids, you're going for more you said," host Tim Russert said to him at the end of the program. "That was your big announcement today."
